pages.hook: Asking the time sounds simple, but in the USA people use a.m. and p.m., half past and quarter after. Learn the small habits so you never miss your bus.

facts.label: The 12-hour clock
facts.sub: 7 a.m. = morning · 7 p.m. = evening. Most people say it this way every day.

facts.label: Two thirty
facts.sub: Also “half past two”. 2:15 can be “quarter after two”.

facts.label: Daylight saving time
facts.sub: In most of the USA the clocks move one hour in March and again in November.

facts.label: Time zones in the lower 48 states
facts.sub: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific. Portland, Oregon, is on Pacific time.

pages.polite: Start with **Excuse me** when you ask a stranger the time. Then say **Thanks!**

mythfact.s: Most people in the USA say the time with a.m. and p.m.
mythfact.why: The 12-hour clock is normal in daily life. The 24-hour clock is used by the military and in some jobs.

mythfact.s: The lower 48 states all share one time zone.
mythfact.why: There are four time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific.

mythfact.s: In most of the USA, clocks change twice a year.
mythfact.why: Daylight saving time starts in March and ends in November. Arizona is a well-known exception.

mythfact.s: “Quarter after three” means 3:45.
mythfact.why: Quarter after three = 3:15. “Quarter to four” = 3:45.

mythfact.s: The nursery rhyme “Hickory Dickory Dock” has a mouse in it.
mythfact.why: The mouse runs up the clock, and the clock strikes one.

lines: Leaves Pine Street: 2:45 p.m. · 3:00 p.m. · 3:15 p.m.

decode.q: You arrive at 2:50 p.m. When is the next bus?
decode.why: The 2:45 bus is gone. The next one is at 3:00 p.m.

lines: Let’s meet at a quarter to seven.

compare.br: In Brazil people say “duas e meia” and often write “14h30” on signs and tickets, so the 24-hour style is easy to see.
compare.us: In the USA you usually say “two thirty” and write 2:30 p.m. Tickets and schedules often show a.m. and p.m., not 14:30.
compare.tip: When you read a schedule, look for a.m. and p.m. first. Then you will not mix up morning and evening.
compare.ask: What time do you wake up? Say it in English with a.m. or p.m.

quiz.q: A stranger can help you. You say…
opts: Excuse me, what time is it?
quiz.why: Excuse me + What time is it? is polite and natural.
A quarter to six = 15 minutes before six = 5:45.

quiz.q: The bus leaves at 8 p.m. Is that morning or evening?
quiz.why: p.m. = after noon. 8 p.m. is evening.

pages.title: Cultural spotlight · Quiz
Reading quest — Just in time at the bus stop · part 1
text: Last Friday I was at a bus stop in **Portland**. I looked at my phone, but the battery was dead. So I asked a woman, “**Excuse me, what time is it?**”
She smiled and looked at her watch. “**It’s two thirty**,” she said. “**Is that the time?**” I said. “My bus is at three o’clock!” I had only thirty minutes, and my friend Carlos was late too.

There was an old clock on the wall of a small cafe, and it made me think of a rhyme. In “Hickory Dickory Dock,” a mouse runs up the clock. The clock strikes one, and the mouse runs down. The rhyme is from 1744, and children still learn it today.

fast.why: The writer asks the time and catches the bus just in time.

scan.q: What time is the bus?
What city is the bus stop in?
What year is the rhyme from?

tf.s: The writer’s phone battery is dead.
The woman says it is three thirty.
The writer drinks a coffee before the bus.
tf.why: “I bought a coffee and sat by the window.”

tf.s: They miss the bus.
tf.why: They got on just in time.

tf.s: Carlos is already at the stop at the beginning.

ctx.why: Just in time = at the last good moment.

pages.title: Reading quest — Just in time at the bus stop · part 2
text: I bought a coffee and sat by the window. **Time flies** when you drink coffee! At ten to three I walked back to the stop. Carlos was there. “Dude, we’re late!” he said. “Chill,” I said. “We have time.”
The bus came at three o’clock, and we got on **just in time**. It was a good day. Now I always check my phone battery in the morning.
